items.title: Mississauga’s next council could decide the future of development around major transit stations in Ward 1
items.summary: The issue is particularly relevant in Ward 1, where Port Credit is already seeing significant development around its GO and future LRT stations. Condo developers have their sights set on the area surrounding the Port Credit GO station, where an underground stop for the new Hurontario LRT is under construction. Mississauga’s next city council could decide the fate of proposed zoning changes that would reshape how much housing and development can be built around 35 major transit station areas (MTSA). On June 10, Mississauga’s planning and development committee approved the proposed pre-zoning changes. However, the implementing zoning bylaw has yet to come before council for a final vote. That means the council elected this fall could ultimately decide whether the new rules actually come into effect. The issue is particularly relevant in Ward 1, where incumbent Coun. Stephen Dasko is in an election race against Olivia Gannon, and where Port Credit is already seeing significant development around its GO and future LRT stations. While there is broad consensus among the two Ward 1 candidates and community representatives that Mississauga needs increased housing closer to transit, concerns remain over how much density neighbourhoods should absorb and how much influence residents may have over individual projects. Dasko, one of the planning and development committee’s 10 members, voted in favour of the proposed pre-zoning changes. However, he said he still has reservations about the changes and would need more information before deciding whether to support the implementing zoning bylaw when it comes before council. Stephen Dasko is running for re-election in Mississauga Ward 1.

items.title: Women in Mississauga, Brampton, Caledon face new digital threats as Take Back the Night returns
items.summary: Women have long been told to watch where they walk after dark, keep their earbuds out and stay alert to what is happening around them. But in 2026, the threats don’t necessarily stop when someone gets home. The internet, social media, online gaming and artificial intelligence have created new ways for sexual and gender-based violence to follow people wherever they go, according to one of the organizers of this week’s Take Back the Night event in Peel Region. The annual rally and march takes place Thursday, Sept. 17, at the TMU Integrated Health Centre at 74 Queen Street West in Brampton, bringing together survivors, advocates, allies and community organizations from across Brampton, Mississauga and Caledon. Rebecca Pacheco, coordinator of the Peel Committee Against Women Abuse (PCAWA) and director of professional practice and advocacy at Embrave Agency to End Violence, said the event is about much more than simply walking through the streets at night. “Take Back the Night is taking back a time that we’re continuously told is dangerous to us,” Pacheco said. Women are routinely given a list of precautions they should take, she said, from walking on the lighted side of the street to avoiding earbuds so they can hear what is happening around them. Instead, she said, the standard should be that everyone is safe regardless of the time of day.

items.title: 2026 TOP 25 CANADIAN IMMIGRANT: Mississauga golfer fosters welcoming space for Black women on the fairway
items.summary: Amaya Athill is one of this year’s Top 25 Canadian Immigrant Award recipients. Amaya Athill is a recipient of the 2026 Top 25 Canadian Immigrant Award. Born in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda, she started playing golf at age five when her father introduced her to the sport. Throughout her teens, she played competitively across the Caribbean, “but neither of my parents had gone to university, so we didn’t know how to navigate getting me a full-ride scholarship,” said the Mississauga resident. Ultimately, Athill ended up attending university in London, England, however, the parameters around golf scholarships were quite different, so she studied law and built a successful career as a barrister instead. , where she focused on civil litigation, international law and human rights. “I didn’t play golf for many years,” Athill said. But when the pandemic hit, she picked up a club and suddenly saw the sport through a new lens.

items.title: Biggest community centre in Mississauga to be transformed
items.summary: Mississauga’s biggest community centre is being reimagined and redeveloped in the next several years to “better meet the needs of a growing community,” the city says. -ft. Mississauga Valley Community Centre and Library, which serves the city’s downtown, is on the books for a major transformation that got underway with a public engagement campaign and community survey this past summer. Design work is slated to begin next year followed by a second public engagement initiative, which will include community presentations and information sessions, on the schedule for late 2027 or spring 2028, according to the City of Mississauga. Officials expect design work to be completed in summer 2029 and construction to begin soon thereafter at a time not yet determined. “Mississauga’s downtown area is a growing community that’s expected to double in size by 2041,” city officials said in an online description of the major project. , is the city’s largest such facility, officials note, adding it was built in 1977 and renovated in 2004. The parkland surrounding the community centre is roughly 50 acres in size and owned by the city.

items.title: Plan to replace plaza with two 16-storey apartment buildings gets approval in Mississauga
items.summary: A plan to replace a Mississauga plaza with two 16-storey apartment buildings gained approval last week. The proposal for 1225 Dundas St. , west of Dixie Road, was approved at the city’s Planning and Development committee on Sept. 8. The plaza is home to a few businesses such as Danforth Food Market, Baituna Furniture and Spoon and Fork. The plan is for two 16-storey apartment buildings connected by a six-storey podium from developers Stephen-Mitchell Reality Limited, Whitehorn Investments Limited, Lynrob Investments Limited, Richco Investments Limited and Tobdele Investments Limited, according to reports submitted to the City of Mississauga. The plaza at 1225 Dundas St. E. in Mississauga. Photo: Google Maps The buildings would contain 553 units with space for businesses on the ground floor. The plans also include 34 four-storey, back-to-back townhouses. Residents are concerned about the proposed buildings’ height and density, shadow impacts on adjacent properties, traffic and parking, construction impacts, landscaping and servicing capacity. Staff said the developer has made adjustments to the plans including reducing the building height and massing, tower stepbacks, increased retail space along the Dundas Street East frontage, the relocation of the indoor amenity area to support a continuous active retail frontage, additional surface parking adjacent to the townhouse blocks, and revisions in response to urban design, wind, sun/shadow and land use compatibility comments.

items.title: Investment scam probe leads to 3 more arrests in Mississauga, elsewhere in Ontario
items.summary: Three additional arrests have been made, including one in Mississauga, as provincial police continue to investigate a 2025 investment scam in which the victim was cheated out of $500,000. The latest pair of arrests came on Sept. 4 and Sept. 10 after Wellington County Ontario Provincial Police officers executed search warrants in Vaughan and London, respectively, police said on Tuesday. On April 16, police made a second arrest in the case, taking one person into custody after executing a search warrant at a Mississauga address. On March 27, police descended on a Brampton home and subsequently arrested one person. The four arrests have been made in connection with a Wellington County OPP fraud investigation that began in October 2025 when officers looked into a reported investment scam involving a victim in Puslinch Township, south of Guelph. Police said the victim is believed to have lost around $500,000. ” In executing the March 27 search warrant in Brampton, police seized a large stash of Canadian cash, high-end clothing and purses, several electronic devices and personal documents, OPP said in a news release on Tuesday.

items.title: Save energy and money with efficient home upgrades
items.summary: Make your home more energy efficient, attend a workshop or check out online resources to learn about programs that can help pay for energy upgrades. Fall is almost here. Now is a good time to prepare your home for cooler weather and explore ways to lower your energy bills. Small changes can help you stay comfortable and save energy without turning up the heat. They will also help to make Mississauga a more climate-friendly city. In 2024, residential buildings across Mississauga produced roughly 15 per cent of the city’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Homeowners can help reduce emissions by making their homes more energy efficient. If you need help getting started, sign up for a home energy coaching session. For example, the Centre for Community Energy Transformation (CCET), a non-profit organization serving Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon, provides a coaching session for free. An energy coach can help you understand your options and create a plan. Toronto and Region Conservation Authority (TRCA) also offers a free one-on-one consultation through its Climate Ready Homes Program, where residents will receive resources to help them save energy and water, reduce waste, create sustainable gardens and improve the comfort of their homes. In addition to these free coaching services, homeowners can also get a more detailed home energy assessment to see where their home is losing energy. This is a paid service offered by independent energy auditors. After the assessment is complete, the auditor will provide the homeowner with a personalized report that identifies upgrades that could help save money and energy.

items.title: #ThanksCoach VIP Box Returns to Mississauga, Celebrating Coaches and Supporting Local Businesses
items.summary: MISSISSAUGA, ON, Sept. 15, 2026 /CNW/ -- The Coaches Association of Ontario (CAO), in partnership with Visit Mississauga, is bringing back the #ThanksCoach VIP Box for a second year. The limited-edition gift box is once again available free of charge to Mississauga coaches and residents. The boxes were pre-ordered by athletes, parents and sport organizations, and delivered as a surprise to coaches at the beginning of National Coaches Week. Following the sellout response to the inaugural 2025 box, this year's features products from a variety of independent Mississauga businesses, many of which are owned or operated by coaches themselves. The initiative shines a light on two integral parts of the Mississauga community - coaches and local businesses - and the important role both play in bringing people together, creating opportunities and building stronger, more connected communities. "The response to the first #ThanksCoach VIP Box was fantastic," said Victoria Clarke, CEO, Visit Mississauga. "Bringing it back for a second year gives us another opportunity to recognize our coaches and our independent businesses. Both give so much back to Mississauga - coaches through the time and energy they dedicate to helping others, and local businesses through the jobs, experiences and connections they create in our community. " "Coaches give so much of themselves to help athletes grow, not just as athletes, but as people," said Jeremy Cross, Executive Director, Coaches Association of Ontario. "The #ThanksCoach VIP Box is a great way to turn that appreciation into action and give people an opportunity to recognize the coaches who have made a difference in their lives. " With 1 in 7 Ontarians actively coaching, coaches represent the largest group of volunteers in the province. In Mississauga, over 68,000 coaches play a vital role in creating opportunities for people of all ages and abilities to participate in sport, build confidence and develop lifelong skills.

items.title: Number of trees planted in Mississauga would form line stretching to Vancouver: city
items.summary: Mississauga officials say the number of trees planted across the city since the launch of the One Million Trees Mississauga initiative in 2013 would, placed end to end, form a line long enough to stretch all the way to Vancouver. In case you’re wondering, the tally of sugar maples, white pines, red oaks, paper birch and other native trees it takes to create such a formation, according to the City of Mississauga, is 653,729. That’s the up-to-date figure (as of this week) of trees planted the past 13 years since the initiative to add one million trees to the city’s canopy by 2032 was launched. The city reached the halfway mark nearly three-and-a-half years ago, in April 2023. Through the program, trees are planted by city staff, community partners and volunteers on both public and private property. The goal is to “help conserve and enhance the city’s open spaces and forested areas for future generations to enjoy,” the city said, adding residents can add to the total one planting at a time if they wish. “Whether you participate in a city tree planting event or plant on your private property, each tree counts. Add your tree to our tally and have it count towards the city’s goal of planting one million trees,” the city said. 2 million trees on both public and private lands across the city. And that number is growing as the municipality, conservation authorities, businesses, community groups, schools and individuals all contribute their tree-planting efforts.
